title: Scheduler policy experiment matrix for quantized runs (interleaving vs batch caps)
creator: Talia Benson
description:
Goal
Establish a repeatable scheduler policy experiment matrix for FP8/INT8 benchmark runs to quantify tradeoffs between prefill/decode interleaving and batch-size caps. We need to answer: which scheduler defaults minimize p95/p99 latency under realistic mixed prompt lengths without materially increasing cost-per-token.

Why
Quantized kernels change per-token timing and can amplify queueing effects. We’ve already seen tail behavior shift on mixed prompt distributions (prefill-heavy + decode-heavy) and under streaming traffic. Kernel-level improvements won’t translate if the scheduler is feeding pathological batch shapes or letting long prefills block decode.

Scope
- Quant modes: FP16 baseline (for control), FP8, INT8
- Workloads: top-hosted streaming chat scenario + at least one non-streaming throughput scenario (see ENG-24811)
- GPUs: H100 + A100 as required; add H200/L40S once provisioned (ENG-24813)
- Scheduler knobs under test (initial set; refine as we learn):
  1) Prefill/decode interleaving policy
     - mode=phase_separated (finish prefill queue slice, then decode)
     - mode=mixed_fair (alternate/fair-share between prefill and decode)
     - mode=decode_priority (bias decode when streaming)
  2) Decode batch caps
     - max_decode_batch_tokens: [4k, 8k, 16k]
     - max_decode_requests_per_batch: [8, 16, 32]
  3) Prefill admission/caps (to reduce head-of-line)
     - max_prefill_batch_tokens: [8k, 16k, 32k]
     - prefill_reservation_ms (time-slice for prefill before yielding to decode): [0, 2, 5]
  4) Backpressure / queue fairness toggles
     - fairness=off vs fairness=on (if supported)
     - stream_decode_reserve=off/on (reserve a small decode budget for active streams)

Deliverables
1) Experiment matrix definition (doc + checked-in config) that benchmark-lab can generate automatically.
2) For each quant mode + GPU: results table for TTFT, TPOT, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, tokens/sec, and queue-wait histograms split by phase.
3) Recommendation for safe defaults (or conditional defaults by GPU/quant mode), with rationale.
4) Notes on failure modes and how to detect them (e.g., TTFT improves but TPOT worsens; throughput increases but queue wait explodes).

Method
- Use pinned runtime build + pinned container + pinned driver settings per benchmark methodology.
- Use the same prompt distribution / concurrency across policy variants.
- For each (GPU, quant mode, policy variant): run N=5 repetitions after warmup; report median and IQR; flag outliers >2.5 IQR.
- Always include FP16 control runs for any new GPU SKU to rule out lab contention.

Instrumentation requirements
- Ensure run output includes scheduler policy knobs and effective caps.
- Require queue-wait breakdown by prefill/decode and streaming vs non-streaming (PR in flight: redwood/pr_10632).
- Emit kernel selection and shapes (ENG-24814 / redwood/pr_10621) to correlate weird batches with kernel choice.

Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Matrix config exists and is runnable via benchmark-lab without manual edits (one command per GPU).
- [ ] Completed runs for: (H100 x {FP16, FP8, INT8}) + (A100 x {FP16, FP8, INT8}) for streaming chat.
- [ ] At least one clear conclusion with supporting data (e.g., “decode cap 8k + mixed_fair reduces TPOT p95 by X% at <Y% throughput loss”).
- [ ] Recommendation written up in sprint report draft (link in ENG-24810) and reviewed by Sofia (scheduling EM) + Noah (perf architect).
- [ ] If a default change is proposed, open follow-up issue with rollout plan + canary gating requirements (ties into ENG-24817).

Links / References
- Umbrella: ENG-24810
- Streaming e2e harness work: ENG-24811
- Scheduler batch-size cap override PR: redwood/pr_10624
- Scheduler instrumentation PR: redwood/pr_10632
- Quant perf canary: perf-canary/pr_188
- Metric definitions ADR: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adr-quant-benchmark-metrics-and-definitions

Open questions
- Do we need separate policies for streaming vs non-streaming routes, or can we use a single default with route overrides?
- Does INT8 benefit from smaller decode batches due to conversion overhead, while FP8 prefers larger batches?
- Are we seeing “prefill hogging” under long-context prompts specifically (ties to ENG-24815), or generally under mixed prompt lengths?

Notes
Initial hypothesis is that quantized decode sees more variance in per-step runtime (kernel selection + conversion paths), which makes large decode batches riskier for tail latency. Expect best tradeoff to be mixed_fair + moderate decode caps, plus a prefill token cap to avoid one long context starving the queue.
comments: 2025-10-03 — Sofia Ivanova: +1 on focusing on queueing effects; make sure we slice results by streaming vs non-streaming. For streaming, TPOT p95 matters more than raw tokens/sec. If we add a "decode_priority" mode, ensure it doesn’t explode TTFT under prefill-heavy traffic.

2025-10-04 — Noah Patel: Please include one control where only decode caps change (keep interleaving constant) so we can attribute deltas cleanly. Also watch for cases where TTFT improves but overall completion latency worsens due to backpressure.

2025-10-06 — Marcus Reed: Drafted initial matrix (3 interleave modes x 3 max_decode_batch_tokens x 2 max_decode_requests) = 18 variants; adding prefill caps makes it too big. Proposal: run a smaller core matrix first, then expand around the best 2 variants with prefill caps.

2025-10-07 — Lena Fischer: For mixed prompt distributions, keep an eye on long-prefill tail: one 24k+ context request can create head-of-line blocking if prefill cap is too high. Recommend testing max_prefill_batch_tokens=16k as a baseline.

2025-10-10 — Marcus Reed: Waiting on redwood/pr_10632 landing in perf-lab build; without queue-wait histograms it’s hard to interpret TPOT regressions. In the meantime, running H100 FP8 with phase_separated vs mixed_fair using existing timing fields.

2025-10-12 — Julian Moore: FYI instrumentation in 10632 now exports queue_wait_ms buckets with tags {phase=prefill|decode, quant_mode, gpu}. Once benchmark-lab includes the new runtime build, you should be able to pull phase split from the structured perf log.
